title: Endocrine Embryology
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter traces where each endocrine gland comes from: the thyroid from the floor of the pharynx, the parathyroids and thymus from the pharyngeal pouches, the pituitary from oral ectoderm and brain, the adrenal from mesoderm and neural crest, and the islets from foregut endoderm. Origin explains adult position, control, and disease. It tells you where ectopic tissue hides, why a midline neck cyst rises with the tongue, why one syndrome links low calcium with T cell deficiency, and why the adrenal medulla and sympathetic chain share tumors. Board questions give the defect, mass, or ectopic site and ask for the embryologic structure behind it.
prerequisites: Germ layers and neural crest derivatives
Pharyngeal arches, pouches, and clefts in the head and neck
Foregut development and rotation of the duodenum (GI-1)
Basic actions of PTH, thyroid hormone, cortisol, catecholamines, and insulin
Hypothalamic control of the pituitary and the hypophyseal portal system

connections.how: The endodermal follicular cell, the C cell, and the pouch-derived chief cell each make a different hormone because each has a different origin.
The thymus shares the third pouch with the inferior parathyroids, so one pouch defect causes both T cell deficiency and hypocalcemia.
Neural crest cells that build the conotruncal septum also populate the pharyngeal arches, which is why 22q11.2 deletion pairs outflow tract defects with pouch defects.
The pituitary sits beneath the optic chiasm and hypothalamus, so a suprasellar mass from Rathke pouch remnants causes field loss and hypothalamic failure.
The islets develop inside the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds, so annular pancreas and pancreas divisum arise from the same process that builds the endocrine pancreas.

A calcitonin-secreting neuroendocrine cell lying between thyroid follicles.
An upgrowth of ectoderm from the roof of the stomodeum (primitive mouth) that forms the anterior pituitary.
A downgrowth from the floor of the diencephalon that forms the pituitary stalk and posterior lobe.
Cells that leave the dorsal neural folds and migrate widely to form sensory and autonomic neurons, melanocytes, chromaffin cells, and much of the facial and pharyngeal mesenchyme.

The large inner zone of the fetal adrenal cortex that makes DHEA sulfate for placental estrogen synthesis and regresses after birth.

sections.title: Thyroid development, descent, and ectopic thyroid

blocks.text: The thyroid is the first endocrine gland to appear, at about day 24, as a thickening of endoderm in the midline floor of the pharynx. The site lies between the two parts of the developing tongue (the tuberculum impar in front and the copula behind) and persists in the adult as the foramen cecum, at the apex of the V-shaped sulcus terminalis that separates the anterior two thirds from the posterior third of the tongue.

The thickening becomes a bilobed diverticulum that descends in the midline in front of the pharyngeal gut, passing anterior to the developing hyoid bone and laryngeal cartilages. Throughout descent it stays attached to the tongue by a narrow channel, the thyroglossal duct. The duct becomes a solid cord and then disappears, and by about week 7 the gland reaches its adult position anterior to the upper trachea as two lateral lobes joined by an isthmus. Follicles containing colloid appear by the end of the third month, when the gland begins to function. Before then the fetus relies on maternal thyroxine (T4) crossing the placenta.

blocks.title: Thyroid descent
steps: Endodermal thickening at the foramen cecum, about day 24
Bilobed diverticulum descends in the midline
Passes anterior to the hyoid and laryngeal cartilages
Thyroglossal duct tethers gland to tongue
Gland lies anterior to trachea by about week 7
Duct involutes; remnants form cyst or pyramidal lobe
blocks.caption: Any thyroid tissue or duct epithelium left behind lies on this single midline track from tongue base to lower neck.

blocks.text: Follicular cell differentiation depends on transcription factors of the primordium, including NKX2-1 (TTF-1), FOXE1, and PAX8. Thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or ectopy) is the main cause of permanent congenital hypothyroidism, and ectopy is its most common form.
Errors of descent and duct closure

Because the whole path is midline, every remnant presents in or near the midline. A lingual thyroid results when the gland fails to descend and stays at the base of the tongue at or near the foramen cecum. It is the most common ectopic site, and in most patients it is the only thyroid tissue present. It often cannot meet demand, so TSH rises and drives growth of the ectopic tissue, which is why a lingual thyroid often enlarges at puberty or in pregnancy and may cause dysphagia, a muffled voice, or airway obstruction.

A thyroglossal duct cyst forms when a segment of duct epithelium persists and fills with secretions. It is the most common congenital midline neck mass and usually sits at or just below the hyoid. Because the tract remains attached to the tongue base, the cyst rises when the tongue is protruded and moves with swallowing. A lateral neck mass along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid instead points to a branchial cleft cyst.

blocks.title: Abnormalities of thyroid descent
rows: Mass at tongue base; often the only thyroid; hypothyroid tendency; TSH-driven growth
Midline tissue above or below the hyoid
Midline mass near hyoid; rises with tongue protrusion; may become infected
Lower duct persists as thyroid tissue
Normal variant above isthmus; enlarges in diffuse goiter
blocks.caption: Every lesion lies on the midline path from the foramen cecum to the lower neck.

blocks.predict: A midline mass at the base of the tongue is found in a 14-year-old girl with a slightly high TSH. Why is the mass enlarging, and why might it be her only thyroid tissue?
blocks.explain: The gland failed to descend from the foramen cecum, so the lingual mass is often the only thyroid present. It cannot meet demand, TSH rises, and TSH drives growth of the ectopic tissue, especially around puberty. Loss of this tissue would leave her with no thyroid at all.

sections.title: Pharyngeal pouch origins of the parathyroids and C cells

blocks.text: The pharyngeal pouches are paired endodermal pockets that push outward from the lateral pharyngeal wall between the arches. Their lining epithelium forms the epithelial part of each derivative, while the surrounding arch mesenchyme, much of it neural crest, forms capsule and connective tissue. The thymus is a good example: its epithelial framework is endoderm, its capsule and septa are neural crest, and its lymphocytes arrive later from bone marrow progenitors.

blocks.title: Pharyngeal pouch derivatives
rows: Middle ear cavity and auditory (pharyngotympanic) tube
Tubotympanic recess; meets the first cleft at the tympanic membrane
Epithelium and crypts of the palatine tonsil
Two halves fuse in the anterior mediastinum
Fuses with thyroid; source of parafollicular C cells
blocks.caption: The numbering runs opposite to the adult position of the parathyroids: third pouch glands end up inferior.

blocks.text: In the fifth week the third pouch splits into a dorsal wing that becomes a parathyroid and a ventral wing that becomes the thymus. Both lose their connection to the pharynx, and the thymus migrates caudally and medially into the anterior mediastinum, pulling the parathyroid with it. The parathyroid separates from the thymus and usually comes to rest on the dorsal surface of the lower thyroid. The fourth pouch parathyroid, which starts lower, makes only a short trip and settles on the dorsal surface of the upper thyroid. The third pouch glands therefore pass the fourth pouch glands and become the inferior parathyroids.

blocks.title: Why third pouch glands end up lowest
steps: Third pouch: dorsal wing parathyroid, ventral wing thymus
Thymus migrates caudally into the mediastinum
Attached parathyroid is pulled down with it
Parathyroid separates near the lower thyroid pole
Fourth pouch parathyroid moves only slightly
Third pouch glands become inferior; fourth become superior
blocks.caption: A long, thymus-dependent migration gives the inferior glands their variable position.

blocks.text: Predicting ectopic glands

The longer and more variable the migration, the more variable the final position. An inferior parathyroid that separates late from the thymus can be found within the thymus or elsewhere in the anterior superior mediastinum; one that separates early or fails to descend may lie high in the neck near the carotid bifurcation, above the superior glands. Superior glands vary much less and, when ectopic, tend to lie posteriorly, in the tracheoesophageal groove or behind the esophagus. Accessory parathyroid tissue and small thymic remnants are also found along the track. This is why a parathyroid adenoma missing from its expected place in the neck is often found in the thymus or anterior mediastinum.
C cells

The ultimobranchial body, from the ventral part of the fourth pouch (sometimes called a rudimentary fifth pouch), fuses with the posterior aspect of the thyroid lobes and disperses its cells among the follicles, where they become parafollicular C cells that secrete calcitonin. Classic teaching, used in most board review sources, holds that these cells originate from neural crest that migrated into the ultimobranchial body. C cells and follicular cells therefore share one gland but not one lineage: medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from C cells, secretes calcitonin, and behaves as a neuroendocrine tumor, while papillary and follicular carcinomas arise from endodermal follicular cells.

sections.title: Dual origin of the pituitary and craniopharyngioma

blocks.text: The pituitary (hypophysis) forms from two separate ectodermal sources that meet. In about the third week, Rathke pouch appears as an upgrowth of oral ectoderm from the roof of the stomodeum, just in front of the oropharyngeal membrane, and grows dorsally toward the brain. At the same time the infundibulum grows ventrally as a downgrowth of neuroectoderm from the floor of the diencephalon. By the end of the second month Rathke pouch loses its connection to the oral cavity as the sphenoid develops between them, and the pouch comes to lie against the infundibulum.

blocks.title: Pituitary development
steps: Rathke pouch rises from the stomodeal roof
Infundibulum descends from the diencephalic floor
The two outgrowths meet
Pouch loses its oral connection by the end of month 2
Anterior wall forms pars distalis; pars tuberalis wraps the stalk
Infundibulum forms stalk and pars nervosa
blocks.caption: Glandular epithelium from the mouth wraps around an extension of the brain.

blocks.text: Cells of the anterior wall of the pouch proliferate to form the pars distalis, the bulk of the anterior lobe (adenohypophysis), and a small extension, the pars tuberalis, grows around the stalk. The posterior wall forms the pars intermedia, which is rudimentary in humans. The remaining lumen narrows to a residual cleft. The infundibulum forms the stalk and the pars nervosa (posterior lobe, neurohypophysis), which contains pituicytes (glial cells) and the axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons.

blocks.title: Anterior and posterior pituitary compared
rows: Neural tissue: axon terminals and pituicytes
GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH
ADH and oxytocin, made in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei
blocks.caption: Origin explains control: the anterior lobe answers to blood-borne releasing hormones, the posterior lobe releases neuronal hormones.

blocks.text: Remnants of Rathke pouch

Epithelial rests can persist along the path of the pouch from the pharyngeal roof to the sella. A Rathke cleft cyst arises from the residual lumen. Craniopharyngioma is a benign but locally aggressive epithelial tumor arising from these rests, usually suprasellar. It has two age peaks, in childhood and in later adulthood. The adamantinomatous type, typical in children, is cystic and calcified, contains thick cholesterol-rich fluid, and is associated with mutations in the beta-catenin gene (CTNNB1). The papillary type, mostly in adults, is rarely calcified and often carries BRAF V600E.

The manifestations follow the location. Pressure on the optic chiasm from above causes bitemporal visual field loss, classically starting in the inferior temporal quadrants. Pressure on the stalk and hypothalamus causes hypopituitarism (growth failure from GH deficiency in a child), central diabetes insipidus from interrupted ADH delivery, mild hyperprolactinemia from loss of dopamine inhibition (the stalk effect), and sometimes hypothalamic obesity. Raised intracranial pressure causes headache. A calcified suprasellar mass in a child is craniopharyngioma until proved otherwise, whereas a pituitary adenoma arises within the sella and is rarely calcified.

blocks.predict: A 9-year-old with headaches and slowing growth develops polyuria with dilute urine. Imaging shows a cystic, calcified mass above the sella. Why does a tumor of anterior pituitary origin cause a posterior pituitary deficit?
blocks.explain: Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke pouch rests but grows above the sella, where it compresses the stalk and hypothalamus. ADH is made in hypothalamic nuclei and travels down the stalk, so compression interrupts its delivery and causes central diabetes insipidus.

sections.title: Two origins of the adrenal gland: mesodermal cortex and neural crest medulla

blocks.text: The adrenal gland is two glands in one capsule. The cortex arises during the fifth week from mesoderm: cells of the coelomic epithelium (mesothelium) on the posterior abdominal wall, between the root of the dorsal mesentery and the developing gonad, proliferate into the underlying mesenchyme. Adrenal and gonadal steroid cells share this adrenogonadal primordium and the transcription factor SF-1, which is why both make steroids from cholesterol with overlapping enzymes, and why small adrenal rests can lie near the gonads or along their path of descent.

The first wave of cells forms a large fetal (provisional) cortex. A second wave surrounds it and forms the thin definitive cortex. The fetal zone lacks much 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity, so it produces large amounts of DHEA sulfate, which the placenta converts to estrogens, chiefly estriol. This fetoplacental partnership makes the fetal adrenal relatively huge, about 10 to 20 times the adult size relative to body weight. After birth the fetal zone regresses rapidly. The zona glomerulosa and fasciculata are present at birth, but the zona reticularis is not recognizable until about the end of the third year.

The medulla forms when neural crest cells from the thoracic region invade the medial side of the fetal cortex and differentiate into chromaffin cells. These cells belong to the same sympathoadrenal lineage as sympathetic ganglion neurons. Each is in effect a postganglionic sympathetic neuron without an axon: it receives preganglionic cholinergic fibers from the thoracic splanchnic nerves, depolarizes through nicotinic receptors, and releases catecholamines into blood instead of onto a target.

blocks.title: How cortical blood shapes medullary output
steps: Arterial blood enters the cortical sinusoids
Blood picks up cortisol at high concentration
Sinusoids drain inward into the medulla
Cortisol induces PNMT in chromaffin cells
PNMT methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine
Medulla secretes mostly epinephrine, about 80%
blocks.caption: Extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue lacks this cortisol-rich blood, so its tumors secrete mainly norepinephrine.

blocks.text: The two origins explain separate disease patterns. Cortical disorders, such as adenomas, carcinomas, and the enzyme defects of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, involve steroid synthesis. Medullary tumors are neural crest tumors of the sympathoadrenal lineage and make catecholamines. Because neural crest cells also form the sympathetic chain and para-aortic chromaffin bodies, the same tumors can arise outside the adrenal anywhere from the skull base to the pelvis, where they are called paragangliomas or extra-adrenal neuroblastomas.

blocks.title: Neural crest tumors of the adrenal medulla
rows: Immature neuroblast of the sympathoadrenal lineage
Malignant; the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood
Episodic or sustained hypertension, headache, sweating, palpitations
Abdominal mass, bone and marrow metastases; hypertension less common
Raised urine homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)
Zellballen nests; RET (MEN2), VHL, NF1, succinate dehydrogenase genes
Small round blue cells, Homer-Wright pseudorosettes; MYCN amplification predicts poor outcome
blocks.caption: Both tumors make catecholamines or their metabolites because both arise from the sympathoadrenal neural crest lineage.

blocks.text: Neuroblastoma rarely causes the dramatic hypertension of pheochromocytoma because its immature cells metabolize much of what they make to HVA and VMA before release. It can also cause opsoclonus-myoclonus, an immune-mediated paraneoplastic syndrome, and occasionally matures spontaneously into a benign ganglioneuroma, behavior that reflects its neural crest identity.

sections.title: 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome: pouch failure, hypocalcemia, and T cell deficiency

blocks.text: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is the most common microdeletion syndrome in humans, occurring in about 1 in 4,000 births and usually arising de novo. The deleted region contains TBX1, a transcription factor gene expressed in pharyngeal endoderm and mesoderm. Its loss disrupts development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches and of the neural crest-dependent pharyngeal arches and cardiac outflow tract. DiGeorge syndrome and velocardiofacial syndrome are names for the same deletion with different emphasis.

blocks.title: Features traced to their embryologic source
rows: Thymic hypoplasia or aplasia: T cell deficiency; absent thymic shadow
Interrupted aortic arch type B, truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot
Cleft palate, velopharyngeal insufficiency, characteristic facies
blocks.caption: The familiar mnemonic CATCH-22 lists cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia from chromosome 22.

blocks.text: Why the newborn develops tetany

Before birth the placenta actively pumps calcium to the fetus, so fetal plasma calcium is higher than the mother's and fetal PTH is low. At birth that supply stops abruptly, and a healthy neonate must raise PTH within the first days to mobilize bone calcium, reduce urinary calcium loss, and stimulate renal calcitriol synthesis. An infant without parathyroid tissue cannot do this, so calcium falls in the first days of life. Phosphate rises because PTH normally promotes phosphate excretion.

blocks.title: From pouch failure to neonatal tetany
steps: 22q11.2 deletion disrupts third and fourth pouches
Parathyroids absent or hypoplastic
Placental calcium supply ends at birth
No PTH response: bone release and calcitriol fall
Ionized calcium falls; phosphate rises
Na+ channels open more easily: tetany, seizures
blocks.caption: Hypocalcemia appears in the first days of life, when the newborn first depends on its own PTH.

blocks.text: Extracellular Ca2+ normally stabilizes nerve membranes by binding to negative charges on the outer surface of voltage-gated Na+ channels. When ionized calcium falls, channels open at a more negative voltage, so peripheral nerves fire spontaneously. The result is jitteriness, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and seizures. In the heart, low calcium lengthens the plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential, which prolongs the ST segment and therefore the QT interval on the ECG.
Why T cells fail but B cells do not

T cell precursors come from bone marrow, but they mature only in the thymus, whose epithelium comes from the third pouch. With little thymic epithelium, few T cells mature. B cell numbers are typically normal because B cells mature in the marrow, but antibody responses that need T helper cells may be weak. Most patients have partial deficiency that improves with age; fewer than 1% have complete athymia, a severe combined immunodeficiency-like state with viral, fungal (including Candida), and Pneumocystis infections. Autoimmunity is also more common, reflecting poor thymic selection.

blocks.title: Reading the neonatal labs
blocks.text: A 3-day-old with a loud murmur has jitteriness and a seizure. Total calcium is 6.4 mg/dL (about 1.6 mmol/L), phosphate is high, magnesium is normal, PTH is low, and the chest film shows no thymic shadow. Low calcium with high phosphate means PTH action is absent, because PTH would lower phosphate. A low PTH during hypocalcemia means the glands cannot respond, so this is hypoparathyroidism, not PTH resistance (which would show high PTH) or vitamin D deficiency (which would show high PTH and low phosphate). Normal magnesium excludes hypomagnesemia, which suppresses PTH release. Combined with a murmur suggesting a conotruncal defect and the absent thymic shadow, the picture points to 22q11.2 deletion.

The pancreas forms from two buds of foregut endoderm at the level of the duodenum. The dorsal bud grows into the dorsal mesentery; the ventral bud arises close to the bile duct. As the duodenum rotates to the right and becomes C-shaped, the ventral bud and bile duct swing behind the duodenum and come to lie below and behind the dorsal bud, and the two buds fuse.

blocks.title: Contributions of the two pancreatic buds
rows: Uncinate process and inferior part of the head
Proximal main pancreatic duct, joining the bile duct at the major papilla
Superior head, neck, body, and tail
Distal main duct; proximal part may persist as accessory duct to the minor papilla
blocks.caption: Failure of the two duct systems to fuse is pancreas divisum; a bifid ventral bud encircling the duodenum is annular pancreas.

blocks.text: Both endocrine and exocrine cells come from the same endodermal progenitors. PDX1 (pancreatic and duodenal homeobox 1) marks all pancreatic progenitors. Cells that switch on neurogenin 3 (NGN3) become endocrine, and further factors such as NKX6.1 and MAFA direct beta cells while ARX directs alpha cells. Islets appear in the third month and scatter throughout the gland, and insulin secretion begins at about the fifth month, with glucagon and somatostatin cells developing from the same parenchyma. Islet cells were once thought to come from neural crest because they share neuroendocrine features, but lineage studies show they are endodermal. Loss of PDX1 on both alleles causes pancreatic agenesis, while one defective copy causes a form of maturity-onset diabetes of the young.

The two buds leave a lasting trace in islet composition. Islets in the posterior head and uncinate process, from the ventral bud, are rich in pancreatic polypeptide (PP) cells and poor in alpha cells, while islets from the dorsal bud are rich in alpha cells. Islets are somewhat more numerous in the tail. Islet tumors, such as insulinoma, arise from these endodermal endocrine cells.
Fetal insulin and maternal diabetes

Fetal insulin acts mainly as a growth factor. Glucose crosses the placenta by facilitated diffusion, but maternal insulin does not, so fetal blood glucose follows the mother's while fetal insulin is set by the fetal beta cells.

blocks.title: Maternal hyperglycemia and the fetal islets
steps: Maternal hyperglycemia
Glucose crosses the placenta; insulin does not
Fetal beta cell hyperplasia and hyperinsulinemia
Insulin drives growth and fat deposition: macrosomia
Cord clamped: glucose supply stops abruptly
High insulin persists: neonatal hypoglycemia
blocks.caption: The same fetal hyperinsulinemia also delays lung surfactant maturation.

blocks.predict: Why does a macrosomic infant of a diabetic mother become hypoglycemic within hours of birth even though the mother's glucose was high?
blocks.explain: The infant's beta cells are hyperplastic from months of high glucose exposure and keep secreting insulin after the cord is cut. The maternal glucose supply ends at once, but the insulin output does not, so glucose falls.

integration.text: Embryology predicts physiology and pathology in this unit. Germ layer identity sets what a cell makes: endodermal follicular and islet cells make iodinated and peptide hormones, mesodermal cortical cells make steroids, and neural crest chromaffin and C cells behave as neuroendocrine cells that secrete amines and calcitonin. Migration predicts location, so ectopic thyroid lies on a midline track, ectopic inferior parathyroids follow the thymus into the mediastinum, and paragangliomas follow the sympathetic chain. Shared origins predict linked defects, as when one pouch defect produces both hypocalcemia and T cell deficiency, or when cardiac neural crest failure adds conotruncal disease.

These rules have limits. Lineage assignments come largely from animal studies, and some classic teachings, such as the neural crest origin of C cells, are under revision. Ectopic positions are tendencies rather than certainties, and 22q11.2 deletion varies widely in severity even within one family, so a missing feature does not exclude the diagnosis.

summary: The thyroid begins at the foramen cecum about day 24, descends in the midline anterior to the hyoid on the thyroglossal duct, and reaches the trachea by about week 7.
Failed descent gives a lingual thyroid, often the only thyroid tissue; a persistent duct gives a midline cyst that rises with tongue protrusion.
Third pouch forms the inferior parathyroids and thymus; fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroids and the ultimobranchial body.
Inferior parathyroids migrate with the thymus, so ectopic glands lie in the thymus or anterior mediastinum; superior glands vary less.
C cells reach the thyroid by way of the ultimobranchial body and are classically neural crest; they give rise to medullary carcinoma.

The anterior pituitary comes from Rathke pouch (oral ectoderm) and is controlled through portal blood; the posterior pituitary comes from the infundibulum (neuroectoderm) and releases hypothalamic hormones.
Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke pouch rests as a calcified suprasellar mass that causes bitemporal field loss, hypopituitarism, and diabetes insipidus.
The adrenal cortex is coelomic mesoderm that makes steroids; the medulla is neural crest that makes catecholamines and gives pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma.
22q11.2 deletion disrupts the third and fourth pouches and pharyngeal neural crest, causing neonatal hypocalcemic tetany, T cell deficiency, and conotruncal defects.
Islets arise from foregut endoderm of both pancreatic buds; maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal beta cell hyperplasia, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

verify: Lineage tracing in mice indicates that thyroid C cells derive from pharyngeal endoderm rather than neural crest; this chapter states the classic neural crest teaching that the registry and most board materials use. Confirm which origin NABNE expects.
The relation of the thyroglossal duct to the hyoid varies (anterior, through, or looping behind the body of the hyoid); the anterior relationship stated here follows the registry and Langman.
The proportion of patients with lingual thyroid who have no other thyroid tissue is quoted from about 70% upward; this chapter says most patients.

Timing values (thyroid primordium about day 24, final position about week 7, colloid by the end of month 3, Rathke pouch about week 3, islets in month 3, insulin at about month 5) follow Langman; other texts differ by about a week.
The incidence of 22q11.2 deletion is quoted from about 1 in 3,000 to 1 in 6,000 births; this chapter uses about 1 in 4,000.
The fraction of pheochromocytomas with a germline mutation is now quoted at about 25% to 40%, replacing the older rule of 10s; confirm the figure NABNE expects.

The example uses a total calcium of 6.4 mg/dL; neonatal hypocalcemia cutoffs (often total calcium below about 8 mg/dL or ionized calcium below about 1.1 mmol/L in term infants) vary by source and gestational age.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the transcription factor names (NKX2-1, FOXE1, PAX8, PDX1, NGN3, TBX1, SF-1) and tumor genetics (CTNNB1, BRAF V600E, MYCN) or only the embryologic origins.
